13.4.6 The WISG 2025 Report stated: ‘Discrimination in the labour market is … widespread. … LGBTQI+ community members—particularly transgender individuals— face systemic inequality in employment. The lack of legal gender recognition mechanisms further exacerbates their exclusion, often forcing them into unofficial or exploitative working conditions.’[footnote 259]

13.4.7 The same report continued: ‘… LGBTQI+ individuals in Georgia struggle to find jobs with dignified conditions. Many are relegated to informal labour with no employment protections, often in the service sector. The state’s discriminatory policies have worsened their already precarious socio-economic conditions, solidifying existing barriers and institutionalizing discrimination in the labour sphere.’[footnote 260]

13.4.8 Equality Movement noted in a statement to the CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025: ‘Since the adoption of the anti-LGBT law, the social and economic exclusion of the LGBTQ+ community has alarmingly intensified. Local community organizations and service providers report incidents such as the dismissal of transgender individuals from workplaces on the basis of their gender identity…’[footnote 261]

13.4.9 Equality Movement noted in a further statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and equally published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month: ‘The “Law on Family Values and Minors” also significantly affects the community’s access to employment as it provides vaguely formulated provision on labor rights exempting employers from anti-discriminatory obligations to respect the person’s gender identity in labor relations …’[footnote 262]

13.4.10 Equality Movement continued in the same statement:

‘The cycle of socio-economic exclusion of the LGBTI community creates significant barriers to their access to the labor market. Studies indicate that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is widespread, occurring both during recruitment processes and throughout employment. In addition, a person’s sexual orientation and/or gender identity often serve as grounds for employment termination. Such barriers often compel LGBTI individuals to hide their identity in the workplace. Equality Movement’s internal “research on the updated needs of the LGBTQ+ community in relation to healthcare, psychosocial and legal services” reveal that for ‘open’ members of the community, the service industry—particularly its entertainment sector—remains the relatively feasible and safe space for employment. However, this sector is characterized by inadequate labor regulations, job instability, and low wages, which contribute significantly to the structural poverty experienced by the community. The cases of labour rights violations processed by Equality Movement’s lawyers frequently involve a person’s illegal dismissal from a work motivated by homophobia.’[footnote 263]

13.4.11 Equality Movement also noted in a statement to the CGRS that was published in the CGRS 2025 Report: ‘… employment opportunities are particularly limited for openly identified [LGBTI] community members. Even within the service industry, which is considered relatively more accessible, they are often subject to exotification—a practice that undermines, rather than supports, genuine emancipation.’[footnote 264]

13.4.12 The Council of Europe’s Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings noted in a report published in October 2025, that individuals of diverse SOGIE ‘…face difficulties in accessing the labour market, as employment opportunities are scarce for those who identify outside the traditional gender binary, leading them to work more in the informal economy (including prostitution) or even to accept abusive job offers.’[footnote 265]

14. Freedom of movement

14.1.1 The WISG 2025 Report observed: ‘… [C]oncerns around safety in public spaces have intensified. Increasingly, activists are avoiding preferred gathering locations and instead opting for alternative venues, choosing to use taxis rather than public transportation to minimize the risk of violence. These adaptations reveal how deeply security concerns are limiting the community’s freedom of movement …, compelling them to adopt restrictive survival strategies.’[footnote 266]

LGBT+ community was estimated to number several thousand people in 2019. In 2018, the NGO Tanadgoma estimated the population of gay men at approximately 18,500. The majority of the LGBT+ community lives in Tbilisi, Batumi and Kutaisi.’[footnote 3]

The first sentence of the quoted paragraph paraphrases a report by the UN’s Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity on his visit to Georgia that was published in May 2019 and noted: ‘… at a rough estimate, the trans community in Batumi could be as high as 100 persons and […] thousands of gay men or men who had sex with men, as well as lesbian and bisexual persons, were active members of social networks.’[footnote 4]

9. Legal framework

9.1 Anti-discrimination provisions

9.1.1 Article 11 of the Constitution of Georgia, adopted in 1995 and most recently amended in 2018, stipulates that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits any discrimination. The article contains a non-exhaustive list of potential discrimination grounds that does not explicitly refer to sexual orientation, gender identity and expression (SOGIE)[footnote 5].

9.1.2 The Law of Georgia on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination, adopted in 2014 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2025, is intended to eliminate every form of discrimination and ensure equal rights of every person under the legislation of Georgia, irrespective of, inter alia, gender and sexual orientation[footnote 6]. Whereas the 2014 version of the law specifically referred to “gender identity and expression” as well[footnote 7], a 2025 amendment deleted this reference[footnote 8].

For information on LGBT+ individuals’ access to services such as healthcare, education, and employment, see Access to services.

9.1.3 Article 2.3 of the Labour Code of Georgia, adopted in 2010 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2025, prohibits any discrimination in labour and pre-contractual relations, including, inter alia, on the grounds of gender and sexual orientation[footnote 9].

For information on accessibility of the labour market for LGBT+ individuals, see Access to employment.

9.1.4 Article 53 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia, adopted in 1999 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2026, provides that the commission of a crime on the basis of sexual orientation constitutes an aggravating circumstance for all crimes under the Code[footnote 10]. Whereas previous versions of the Criminal Code also listed “gender” and “gender identity” as aggravating reasons for intolerance[footnote 11], a 2025 amendment deleted these references[footnote 12].

9.2 Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union

9.2.1 Article 30 of the Constitution of Georgia, defines marriage as a union of a woman and a man for the purpose of founding a family[footnote 13]. This definition was introduced by the 2017 law On Amendments to the Constitution of Georgia[footnote 14].

9.2.2 Similarly, article 4 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors, adopted in 2024, defines marriage in Georgia as a voluntary union exclusively between a man and a woman for the purpose of forming a family. It explicitly prohibits the registration or legal recognition of same-sex unions as marriage, including those concluded abroad which have no legal validity in Georgia[footnote 15].

9.2.3 Article 5 of the same law prohibits the adoption of a child by a non-heterosexual person[footnote 16]. The prohibition is replicated in article 4 of the Law of Georgia on Adoption and Foster Care[footnote 17].

9.2.4 The undated International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA) World Database entry for Georgia indicated that ‘[t]he Criminal Code (2000) of Georgia removed the pre-existing sodomy provisions that were carried through from the Soviet Union period’[footnote 18], thus decriminalising consensual same-sex sexual acts.

9.3 Trans rights

9.3.1 Article 5 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits the adoption of a child by a person that does not identify with a biological sex or that identifies with a sex different from their biological sex[footnote 19].

9.3.2 Article 6 of the same law prohibits procedures intended to assign or reassign an individual to a different sex through medical means[footnote 20].

9.3.3 Article 176 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia defines the punishment for the performance of a surgical operation or other medical treatment intended to assign an individual to a different sex as a fine, an occupational ban of up to three years, or imprisonment for one to four years[footnote 21]. See Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people.

9.3.4 Article 7 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits registering or later changing a person’s sex in civil status records to anything other than their biological sex. It also prohibits indicating a different sex in identity documents or other official state-issued documents as well as recognising or enforcing foreign court decisions that assign a person a non-biological or non-binary sex[footnote 22].

9.4 Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism

9.4.1 Article 3 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors defines the term ‘popularisation’ as the positive or exemplary portrayal of same-sex relationships as well as of identification with a sex different from one’s biological sex or with a non-binary sex[footnote 23].

9.4.2 Article 8 of the same law prohibits ‘popularisation’ as defined in article 3 in educational institutions[footnote 24].
